Turtle Lake and Vake Park

The city's green axis — from Vake Park up by cable car to Turtle Lake, where Tbilisi actually relaxes.

Time needed
2 h
From Tbilisi
9 km · 0:20
Road
Paved
Car needed
Economy class
Season
All year
Entry
free

Turtle Lake belongs to the locals. It rarely tops a visitor's list, and that is precisely why it delivers something the Old Town cannot: ordinary, unperformed Tbilisi. The small lake sits at 686 metres on a pine-covered ridge above Vake.

Vake Park below was laid out in 1946 and is a textbook Soviet park — broad alleys, a fountain, a cascade of steps. From its upper end a cable car climbs to the lake in about five minutes, with the whole district dropping away beneath you.

What people do at Turtle Lake:

  • Walk the flat lakeside loop, roughly a kilometre around
  • Rent a pedalo or rowing boat in the warm months
  • Sit in the terraced cafés looking out over the water towards the ridge
  • Walk down to the Open Air Museum of Ethnography, about twenty minutes on a woodland path
  • In winter, simply walk: the lake often freezes at the edges and the pine forest goes quiet

Because the ridge is one of the coolest spots in Tbilisi, half the city comes up here during the July and August heat. Mid-week is when you get the place closer to how it feels the rest of the year, and the light on the water in late afternoon is worth the trip on its own.

Practical advice

In summer the lakeside cafés fill after five in the afternoon and parking becomes the main problem — either come early or take the cable car up from Vake Park instead. The lake is not an official swimming spot even though people do swim; there is no supervised beach. Dress for the evening drop in temperature up here. ATMs are down on Chavchavadze, and not every kiosk by the lake takes cards. With children this is one of the easiest days out in the city.

How to get there from Tbilisi

Follow Chavchavadze Avenue to Vake Park, then either leave the car at the park and ride the cable car, or keep driving the switchbacks straight to the lake — both take up to twenty minutes from the centre. There is free parking around the lake, though on summer evenings it is full and the narrow road makes passing awkward. The surface is asphalt the whole way. In winter the climb needs careful driving when it ices over, but no four-wheel drive is required; an economy car is enough.
